title: Ageing
hookLine: a grandparent who won't accept help, and the Buddha's own word for his old body: a worn-out cart
tomorrow: a king, a barber, one gray hair. what happens next?

cards: Somebody's grandparent bristles when you take the heavy bag from their hands: I'm not that old. It's a little standoff, pride on one side and worry on the other, and both of them are love.
The Buddha was old too, and he didn't bristle. Near the end of his life, the long sutta of his last days says, he told Ananda plainly: I am old now, my journey is near its end, I am turning eighty.
And then he chose a picture for his own body. A worn-out cart.

teach.b: The full picture is this: just as an old cart keeps going only with straps and bindings holding it together, so, he says, this body keeps going only by being held together.
There's no shame in the line, and no drama. It's a plain report from someone who has looked carefully. The cart is old.
It needs straps. It still moves. And straps are not defeat.
A cart tied with care can still carry its load down the road, and the Buddha kept walking and teaching for some time after he said this.

Right after, in the same passage, he tells Ananda to be an island to himself and a refuge to himself, with the teaching as his island and refuge. The old cart is not the thing to lean on forever; the practice is.
So here's what the tradition gives a family in the middle of the bag standoff. First, honesty: the body ages, even the Buddha's, and saying so out loud is not an insult.
Second, the straps: a cane, a raised bench, a hand on the stairs are not a loss of dignity; they're how old carts keep going.
Third, the load: what matters is what the cart still carries, the kindness, the stories, the teaching handed on.
Something to tell someone tonight: the Buddha used a cart held together with straps to describe himself.

how: Buddhist monasteries and families often care for their elders at home; reflecting on one's own ageing is one of the five daily recollections many Buddhists recite.

o: the body growing old, met honestly and without shame
a stage of life that monks believe they can avoid
a punishment for mistakes made earlier in life

games.q: the old cart — tap the pairs.
p: what holds an old body together
what an old cart still carries

s: the Buddha's body stayed young because of his practice
he called it an old cart held together with straps.
right after the cart picture, the Buddha told Ananda to be an island to himself
with the teaching as his island and refuge.
needing help with an old body is a failure on the path
straps are how old carts keep going; the Buddha said so of himself.

games.q: your grandmother refuses a cane because 'it makes me look old.' what fits the old cart?
o: agree; hiding age is how to stay dignified.
a cane is a strap: the cart is old, and it still carries her where she wants to go.
insist hard until she gives in; safety is all that matters.
games.why: the Buddha described his own body as an old cart kept going with straps, with no shame in it.

practice: Count, slowly, things this body has carried you through: a long walk, a hard week, someone you held. Let each one land with a quiet thank you to the body, whatever its age or its aches.
If the count runs out, start again from the first, and thank it twice.

wordCard.voice: Ageing: the body as an old cart, held together with straps, honest about its age, still carrying something worth carrying.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: jara, old age, decay.

carryVoice: Here is the picture: the old cart, strapped with care, still on the road. Six of nine.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta, 2.25-26: 'I am old, ... turning eighty'; the body kept going like a worn-out cart held together with straps; be an island and refuge to yourself, with the Dhamma as island and refuge)
